asr_transcript: Metalicity means oxygen abundance in star-forming gas. Nearby galaxies define a mass-metallicity relation at each stellar mass. This paper asks whether galaxies at redshift 9 to 10 fall below that local relation. Two problems can blur the test. Lensing may magnify compact glowing gas differently from broader starlight used to estimate mass. The common local comparison is also extrapolated below the stellar mass range where it was calibrated. The core evidence is five strictly unlunzed pollute galaxies from redshift 9.3 to 9.9. Their oxygen abundances use direct electron temperature measurements, which infer gas temperature from an auroral line. A DEX is a logarithmic unit. Against the CURDY comparison, the five galaxies average 0.69 plus or minus 0.03 DEX lower in oxygen abundance, leaving about 1 fifth the nearby level. Leave one out tests show a 0.04 DEX spread. Replacing the extrapolated CURDY comparison with the Andrews and Martini relation measured at these masses moves the deficit from 0.69 to about 0.65 DEX. The 0.04 DEX shift is roughly 10%. GNZ11 is not among the five core pollute galaxies. It is a separate extension at redshift 10.6 with greater oxygen abundance uncertainty. It confirms the deficit's direction while the population result remains 0.64 to 0.68 DEX lower. A separate cross check stacks roughly 1,500 unlens JADES galaxies across redshift 4 to 10. It finds a 0.5 to 0.6 DEX deficit, only one quarter to one third the nearby abundance. The redshift 9 to 10 value still rests on individual pollute detections. The electron temperature scale remains uncertain by 0.1 to 0.2 DEX. The deficit's direction survives checks, but its size is systematics limited. This machine generated draft is descriptive, not validated, and not a detection. Automated review is not journal or human peer review.
